findings.title: Cayman CRS 2.0 – 2025 Filing Deadline July 31, 2026
findings.summary: Cayman Financial Institutions must file their 2025 CRS Returns and Declarations by July 31, 2026. Following this deadline, the DITC Portal will be temporarily closed in early August 2026 to facilitate the transition from CRS XML Schema v2.0 to v3.0. The new CRS reporting deadline for the 2026 reporting period shifts to June 30, 2027, and the DITC is expected to release updated CRS 2.0 guidelines in Q3 2026.
findings.client_impact: Any FGC client holding accounts or fund interests through Cayman-regulated financial institutions must confirm that their institution has filed its 2025 CRS return — and that the client's account data is correctly reported — before the portal closes on July 31. Failure to file exposes institutions to DITC enforcement and could affect account standing.
findings.urgency_reason: Deadline is July 31, 2026 — four days from today. This is the hardest time-bound compliance event in the batch and requires immediate verification with Cayman-based counterparts.

findings.title: Cayman Tokenised Fund Legislation in Force (March 2026)
findings.summary: The Mutual Funds (Amendment) Act, 2026 and the Private Funds (Amendment) Act, 2026 came into force on March 24, 2026, establishing clear rules for tokenised mutual and private funds. Tokenised funds are regulated in the same manner as traditional funds with added requirements for digital equity or investment tokens. The Virtual Asset (Service Providers) (Amendment) Act, 2026 clarified that digital equity and investment tokens issued by these funds are excluded from the VASP regime.
findings.client_impact: HNW clients investing in or considering tokenised fund structures in Cayman now have a clear regulatory framework governing their investments, with digital equity and investment tokens explicitly outside the VASP regime. Clients exploring digital asset exposure via fund wrappers should review structuring options against the new legislation.
findings.urgency_reason: In force since March 2026 — no immediate deadline, but FGC advisors should be conversant with the new framework when clients raise tokenised fund interest. Classified WATCH rather than FYI given the pace of client demand in this space.

findings.title: Beneficial Ownership and Transparency Act 2026 Extends to Private and Mutual Funds
findings.summary: The Cayman Islands' Beneficial Ownership and Transparency Act 2026 expanded disclosure obligations to previously exempt structures, including private and mutual funds. This represents a significant broadening of the UBO regime beyond corporate entities to fund vehicles commonly used by wealth management clients.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients using Cayman private or mutual funds as holding or investment vehicles — previously exempt from UBO disclosure — are now within scope and must ensure their beneficial ownership data is correctly registered. Advisors should audit client fund structures for compliance gaps.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the Act is already in force but compliance timelines and operational details are still being absorbed by fund administrators. No single imminent filing deadline was identified, but non-compliance exposure is active and growing.

findings.title: BVI Legitimate Interest Access to UBO Register Now Active (April 2026)
findings.summary: Since April 1, 2026, persons and institutions demonstrating a 'legitimate interest' connected to AML, counter-terrorist financing, or counter-proliferation financing can access BVI beneficial ownership information — including name, month/year of birth, nationality, and nature of interest — for individuals owning or controlling 25% or more. The regime does not constitute a publicly available register.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients relying on BVI structures for privacy now face a materially higher risk of UBO disclosure to law enforcement and AML-credentialed third parties; the register is not public but is no longer closed. Clients should review whether their BVI vehicles remain fit for purpose given their personal risk tolerance and profile.
findings.urgency_reason: Active since April 2026 — the legal exposure is live, but no additional compliance action is required from clients at this stage. Classified WATCH because the policy is new and the practical use of legitimate-interest access is still evolving.

findings.title: OECD Pillar Two Side-by-Side Safe Harbor for US Multinationals – Effective 2026
findings.summary: On January 5, 2026, the OECD Inclusive Framework agreed a Side-by-Side Safe Harbor that exempts US-parented multinational groups from the Income Inclusion Rule and Undertaxed Profits Rule, based on the sufficiency of US domestic tax law. Effective for fiscal years beginning on or after January 1, 2026. The US is currently the only jurisdiction listed in the OECD Central Record qualifying for this arrangement.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients who are US citizens or tax residents holding foreign subsidiaries or MNE groups may now qualify for this safe harbor, substantially reducing Pillar Two compliance complexity and cost — but the analysis must be done structure-by-structure, as qualification depends on the specific US tax footprint. Non-US clients holding US-parented groups are similarly affected.
findings.urgency_reason: Effective January 1, 2026, so the safe harbor is operative for the current fiscal year. Classified WATCH because clients should factor this into 2026 tax planning and any ongoing Pillar Two readiness work, even though no individual client deadline is imminent.

findings.title: OECD GloBE Information Return XML Schema v3.0 Guidance Released (June 2026)
findings.summary: In June 2026, the OECD released guidance on the GloBE Information Return (GIR) XML Schema for the first GloBE filing and exchange cycle, containing practical fixes, workarounds, and the switch-off of certain validation rules. Directly relevant to Cayman, Luxembourg, and other jurisdictions with Pillar Two-compliant MNE structures.
findings.client_impact: Clients with MNE structures subject to GloBE reporting should confirm that their tax compliance providers are using the v3.0 schema and have applied the OECD's documented workarounds to avoid validation failures on first filing. This is primarily an operational/compliance matter for their tax advisors.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because this is technical operational guidance for compliance teams rather than a strategic client planning issue. No client-facing deadline is triggered by this release alone.

findings.title: Brazil UBO Digital Filing (e-BEF) Mandatory – First Deadline December 31, 2026
findings.summary: Normative Instruction No. 2,290/2025, effective January 1, 2026, introduced the e-BEF (Digital Beneficial Ownership Form) for all Brazilian entities including companies, associations, cooperatives, foundations, investment funds, and financial institutions. The first annual filing deadline under the new system is December 31, 2026. UBO data may be shared with foreign tax authorities under CRS/FATCA reciprocity agreements.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients who are UBOs of Brazilian-registered entities — companies, funds, foundations — must ensure their Brazilian legal counsel registers accurate e-BEF data before December 31, 2026, or risk penalties and potential disclosure of their ownership information to foreign tax authorities via CRS/FATCA exchanges.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the December 31, 2026 deadline is five months away, providing a planning window — but e-BEF registration requires gathering UBO documentation and engaging local counsel, and many Brazilian entities have not yet started preparation.

findings.title: BCB Resolution 521/2025 – New FX Framework for VASPs and Stablecoins
findings.summary: BCB Resolution 521/2025, in force February 2, 2026, integrates crypto/VASP operations into Brazil's foreign exchange framework. From October 2026, financial institutions may not provide banking or FX services to unauthorised VASPs. A new monthly reporting regime covering stablecoin purchases, sales, and international transfers commences November 3, 2026.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients holding stablecoins or using crypto-native payment rails for cross-border transfers involving Brazil face significant disruption if their counterparty VASPs are not BCB-authorised by October 2026; any such transfers must be reviewed now and alternative arrangements made if necessary. The November reporting regime will also require detailed counterparty data for each international crypto transfer.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the banking-service cut-off (October 2026) and reporting commencement (November 3, 2026) are three to four months away — close enough to require proactive client review of their Brazilian crypto and FX arrangements now.

findings.title: CVM Resolution 175 Fully in Force for All Brazilian Investment Funds
findings.summary: As of July 1, 2026, all Brazilian investment funds must comply with CVM Resolution 175, a unified regulatory framework modernising the fund industry. CVM's 2026 Regulatory Agenda also includes priority revisions affecting FIPs (private equity), FIFs (fixed income), FIIs (real estate), and actively managed ETFs, plus a crowdfunding regulation overhaul.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients invested in Brazilian FIPs, FIIs, or other fund types must confirm that their fund managers have completed the transition to CVM 175 and that fund documents have been updated — non-compliant structures may face regulatory sanctions affecting fund operations and distributions. Further amendments are expected this year and should be tracked.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the compliance deadline (July 1, 2026) has just passed, making this an active enforcement window. Clients who have not yet confirmed their fund managers' compliance should do so immediately.

findings.title: Switzerland LETA – Federal UBO Register to Enter Force October 1, 2026
findings.summary: The Federal Act on the Transparency of Legal Entities (LETA) and revised Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA) enter into force October 1, 2026, creating a central federal Transparency Register. Swiss legal entities and certain foreign entities with a Swiss nexus must register UBO information at the ≥25% ownership or control threshold, aligning Switzerland with FATF standards.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients with Swiss companies, foundations, or other legal entities must register their beneficial ownership data by the effective date — October 1, 2026 — or face penalties; foreign entities with Swiss nexus (e.g., branch offices or Swiss-managed structures) are also in scope and must determine whether they fall within the registration obligation.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the October 1, 2026 effective date is 66 days away. Preparation requires identifying all in-scope entities, gathering UBO documentation, and filing through the new register — a process that should begin immediately.

findings.title: FINMA Launched Consultation on Revised AMLO-FINMA (May-June 2026)
findings.summary: FINMA ran a consultation on the partially revised Anti-Money Laundering Ordinance (AMLO-FINMA) from May 12 to June 9, 2026, reinforcing requirements to understand client structure, strengthening payable-through account rules, and incorporating new sanctions/embargo compliance obligations.
findings.client_impact: Swiss-regulated financial intermediaries (banks, asset managers) serving FGC clients will be subject to enhanced CDD obligations once the revised AMLO-FINMA is finalised — this may result in additional documentation requests from Swiss counterparties. No immediate client action is required until the final ordinance is published.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the consultation period has closed and the final rule has not yet been published. This is a developing situation worth monitoring but no client action is required today.

findings.title: MAS Consults on CIS Code Amendments for New Retail Fund Types (July 9, 2026)
findings.summary: On July 9, 2026, MAS published a consultation paper on proposed amendments to the Code on Collective Investment Schemes (CIS Code) to enable a wider range of new fund product types to be authorised for retail offer through a more streamlined process, while maintaining retail safeguards.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients with Singapore-based fund investments or those considering Singapore-domiciled fund structures may benefit from expanded product availability once the amendments are finalised, but no immediate action is required. FGC advisors tracking fund innovation should monitor the outcome of this consultation.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because this is a consultation at an early stage — no rule change has been adopted yet and the direct client impact is prospective. Singapore is a secondary jurisdiction for FGC's core Latin American HNW client base.

findings.title: UAE Capital Markets Authority (CMA) Replaces SCA – New Framework from January 2026
findings.summary: Federal Law No. 32 and 33 of 2025 reconstituted the SCA as the Capital Market Authority (CMA) and introduced a new Capital Markets Law framework, both effective January 1, 2026. Key changes include statutory prospectus liability, significantly higher penalties, a recovery and resolution regime, and extraterritorial reach to persons targeting UAE clients from outside the UAE.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients — or FGC itself — who offer investment products or advice to UAE-resident clients are now potentially subject to UAE CMA jurisdiction even if operating from abroad; advisors should review whether any client engagements or marketing activities directed at UAE clients require CMA authorisation or compliance steps under the new framework.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the extraterritorial scope of the new law is significant and potentially affects FGC's advisory activities, but the full enforcement posture of the new CMA is still becoming clear. Advisors should seek a legal opinion if they have UAE-resident clients.

findings.title: Panama Law 526 – New Economic Substance Requirements for Multinational Groups (Enacted May 2026)
findings.summary: Law 526, enacted May 28, 2026, introduces economic substance requirements for Panamanian entities that are part of multinational groups and earn passive foreign-source income. Entities failing to demonstrate genuine substance face a 15% tax on net taxable income effective January 1, 2027. Implementing regulations are due within 90 days of enactment (by approximately August 26, 2026).
findings.client_impact: FGC clients using Panamanian holding companies or SPVs to receive passive income — dividends, interest, royalties, capital gains — from multinational group operations must now plan to demonstrate genuine economic substance in Panama by January 1, 2027; the upcoming implementing regulations (expected by late August 2026) will define exactly what qualifies, making the next 30 days a critical window for strategy review.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the effective date (January 1, 2027) allows a planning window, but the implementing regulations are due in approximately 30 days — which will define the substance standards clients must meet. FGC advisors with Panama-structured clients should engage Panamanian counsel immediately to prepare.

findings.title: Cyprus Comprehensive Tax Reform Effective January 1, 2026
findings.summary: Cyprus enacted a major tax reform effective January 1, 2026: corporate income tax raised from 12.5% to 15%; SDC on dividends reduced from 17% to 5% for Cyprus tax-resident and domiciled individuals; crypto asset gains taxed at 8%; loss carry-forward extended from 5 to 7 years; Deemed Dividend Distribution rules abolished. The non-domicile regime remains intact.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients using Cyprus holding companies face a higher CIT rate (now 15%, aligned with Pillar Two) but benefit from a dramatically lower dividend SDC (5% vs 17%) if they are Cyprus-resident and domiciled — the net effect must be modelled per client. Non-domicile clients remain fully exempt from SDC, preserving the regime's core attraction for international HNW clients.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because these changes took effect January 1, 2026, and any client with a Cyprus holding structure whose tax planning was not updated at year-end may be operating under incorrect assumptions. Advisors should confirm that clients' Cyprus structures have been reviewed in light of the new rates.

findings.title: Bahamas Enacts Usufruct Interest Act, 2026 – New Wealth Structuring Tool
findings.summary: The Bahamas enacted the Usufruct Interest Act, 2026 on March 23, 2026, establishing the jurisdiction's first comprehensive statutory usufruct framework. The Act enables formal separation of beneficial enjoyment from legal ownership over a broad asset class including equity interests, securities, intellectual property, digital assets, receivables, and real property. Usufruct interests may be publicly registered.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients engaged in succession planning or intergenerational wealth transfer now have access to a formally registered Bahamian usufruct as an alternative to trusts or foundations, particularly useful for separating income rights from capital rights across generations or for cross-border estate structures where forced heirship rules in the client's home jurisdiction might otherwise complicate planning.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because this is a new and potentially valuable structuring tool for estate planning clients, not an obligation. Advisors working on succession mandates should consider whether a Bahamian usufruct fits the client's needs.

findings.title: Bahamas Central Bank Publishes TF and PF National Risk Assessments – July 2026
findings.summary: The Central Bank of The Bahamas released the Terrorist Financing NRA 2024 and Proliferation Financing NRA 2025 in July 2026. These risk assessments inform updated AML/CFT/CPF obligations for supervised financial institutions in The Bahamas.
findings.client_impact: Bahamian-regulated institutions holding client accounts or fund interests may tighten CDD procedures or introduce enhanced due diligence for higher-risk client categories based on the NRA findings; FGC clients with Bahamian accounts or fund structures should be prepared for potential KYC refresh requests from their Bahamian counterparties.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the NRAs inform future regulatory changes rather than imposing immediate obligations on clients directly. No specific deadline is triggered by the publication.

findings.title: Isle of Man Lowers UBO Threshold to 25% (Effective May 25, 2026)
findings.summary: Amendments in force from May 25, 2026 lower the Isle of Man's registrable beneficial ownership threshold from 'more than 25%' to '25% or more', bringing individuals holding exactly 25% into scope. A more detailed, judgment-based approach to control assessments for trusts, foundations, and governance arrangements was also introduced. Nominated officers must adopt the new process by September 15, 2026.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients with Isle of Man entities where any individual holds precisely a 25% stake must ensure their beneficial ownership register is updated to include those individuals; clients using IoM trusts or foundations should also expect their fiduciary service providers to apply the new judgment-based control test and may receive requests to clarify governance arrangements.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH with near-term urgency: the September 15, 2026 deadline for nominated officers to adopt the new process is approximately 50 days away, and any affected IoM entity should be actioning this now.
findings.source_name: Charterhouse Lombard / Isle of Man Government

findings.title: Jersey and Guernsey Propose Legitimate Interest Access to UBO Registers
findings.summary: Both Jersey and Guernsey are advancing proposals to extend access to their central beneficial ownership registers to persons demonstrating a legitimate interest connected to AML, counter-terrorist financing, and proliferation financing — mirroring the BVI's April 2026 activation and the Isle of Man's similar consultation.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients with Jersey or Guernsey structures who rely on register access restrictions for privacy should note that these proposals — if enacted — would expose beneficial ownership data to AML-credentialed investigators and potentially journalists with demonstrated public interest; the shift is directional across all Crown Dependencies and should factor into long-term structuring decisions.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because these are proposals, not enacted law, but the legislative direction is clear and consistent with the wider Crown Dependencies trend. Advisors should monitor for passage and estimated timelines.

findings.title: Luxembourg SPF Regime Expanded – Now Available as Simplified Joint-Stock Company
findings.summary: A Luxembourg law dated December 19, 2025 allows SPFs (private wealth management companies) to be established as sociétés par actions simplifiées (simplified joint-stock companies), expanding structuring flexibility. The minimum annual subscription tax was also raised from EUR 100 to EUR 1,000, with administrative fines up to EUR 250,000 for violations.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients considering Luxembourg as a wealth-holding jurisdiction now have a more flexible SPF corporate form available, potentially better suited to complex shareholder arrangements than the traditional SA or Sàrl; however, the subscription tax increase (10x) and new penalty regime make ongoing compliance more material and requires annual filings to be taken seriously.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the expanded structuring option is immediately available and material for clients in ongoing Luxembourg planning discussions. The subscription tax change is already in effect.

findings.title: Luxembourg AIF Carried Interest Tax Regime – New Rules for 2026 Tax Year
findings.summary: Draft law No. 8590 introduces a new tax regime for carried interest granted to managers of alternative investment funds (AIFs) in Luxembourg, expected to apply from the 2026 tax year.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients who are Luxembourg AIF managers — or who have co-investment rights linked to carried interest in Luxembourg-domiciled private equity or real asset funds — should obtain a specific tax analysis of how the new regime applies to their compensation or co-investment structure before year-end 2026, as the tax treatment may differ materially from prior years.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the regime is expected to apply for the 2026 tax year currently in progress, but the draft law is not yet final. Clients with Luxembourg fund management or co-investment exposure should instruct local counsel to monitor and advise promptly upon enactment.

findings.title: US Federal Estate Tax Exemption Made Permanent at $15M per Person (OBBBA)
findings.summary: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed July 4, 2025, made the TCJA's elevated estate and gift tax exemptions permanent and raised them to $15 million per person ($30 million per married couple) effective January 1, 2026, indexed for inflation from 2027. Non-resident aliens retain only a $60,000 federal estate tax exemption for US-situs assets.
findings.client_impact: The elimination of the 2026 sunset fundamentally changes the planning calculus for FGC's US-citizen clients — strategies designed to 'use it before you lose it' may now be unnecessary or even sub-optimal and should be reviewed. Conversely, FGC's non-US resident clients holding US situs assets (real estate, US equities) remain exposed to US estate tax with only a $60,000 exemption, a gap that has never been wider relative to the US-citizen exemption and demands active estate planning.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because while the exemption change is effective January 1, 2026, many clients' estate plans were structured around the anticipated sunset and have not yet been reassessed. This is an active advisory opportunity and risk for the current year.

findings.title: FinCEN BOI: Domestic US Companies Remain Exempt; Foreign-Formed Entities Must File
findings.summary: Following FinCEN's March 21, 2025 interim final rule, all US-formed entities and their beneficial owners are exempt from BOI reporting under the CTA. Only foreign-formed companies registered to conduct business in the US must report. A final rule is expected in 2026 and could expand or confirm the current scope.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients with foreign-registered entities (e.g., Cayman, BVI, or Luxembourg companies) that are also registered to do business in a US state must file BOI reports with FinCEN — the exemption applies only to US-formed entities. Clients should audit any foreign entity with US state registrations and confirm compliance.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified WATCH because the obligation for foreign-registered entities is current and active, and the pending final rule may alter scope. A final rule in 2026 could re-expand reporting requirements to domestic entities, requiring rapid response.

findings.title: Florida SB 264 – Foreign Buyer Restrictions Remain in Force; Legal Challenges Ongoing
findings.summary: Florida SB 264 (effective July 1, 2023) restricts nationals from designated 'countries of concern' (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Venezuela, Syria) from acquiring certain real property in Florida. The law remains in force in 2026. Federal courts have halted enforcement against some individual Chinese plaintiffs pending appeal, but the Eleventh Circuit has otherwise upheld the law. All foreign nationals must complete an affidavit at closing.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients who are nationals of — or have significant ties to — any of the seven designated countries must receive specific legal advice before acquiring Florida property; all other foreign national clients must complete a closing affidavit confirming they are not within the restricted categories. FGC's core Latin American client base is generally not affected by the nationality restrictions but should be advised of the affidavit requirement.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because the law has been in force since 2023 and there are no new filing deadlines or rule changes in the current period. Legal challenges are ongoing but have not suspended the law for most buyers.

findings.title: FIRPTA Withholding Remains at 15% for Foreign Sellers; Non-Resident Estate Exemption $60K
findings.summary: FIRPTA withholding for foreign persons selling US real property interests remains at 15% of gross sales price for 2026, with no rate changes. Non-resident alien estate tax exemption for US-situs assets is $60,000, versus the $15 million exemption now available to US persons under the OBBBA.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients who are foreign sellers of US real estate should budget for a 15% FIRPTA withholding at closing (recoverable via tax return if actual gain is lower) and should confirm that their US tax counsel has a withholding certificate strategy in place. The $60,000 non-resident estate exemption compared to the new $15M US-citizen exemption highlights a critical planning gap for international clients holding US situs assets — estate planning documents for these clients should be reviewed.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because there are no FIRPTA rate changes — this is a status-quo reminder. The estate tax contrast with the OBBBA $15M exemption is the more actionable planning point, covered separately under the OBBBA finding.

findings.title: MFSA Investment Services Regulatory Briefing Covers July 2025–February 2026 Period
findings.summary: The Malta Financial Services Authority issued its latest Investment Services Supervision Regulatory Briefing covering July 2025 to February 2026, highlighting stronger governance, enhanced transparency, and granular supervisory reporting as regulatory priorities for 2026. Malta's MiFID II passporting guidelines were also updated.
findings.client_impact: FGC clients invested in Malta-regulated funds or using Malta-based investment managers should expect their counterparties to implement enhanced governance and reporting processes in 2026, which may result in updated documentation or reporting requests. No immediate client-facing obligation is triggered.
findings.urgency_reason: Classified FYI because this is a supervisory briefing covering past developments and signalling priorities — no specific client deadline or material rule change is identified that requires immediate action.
